Name: CSV
Description:
A comma separated value (CSV) file is a text file representing tabular data.

Each line represents a separate row and each column is separated by some delimiter character, usually a comma.

Share.explanation:
CSV files are good for sharing data because they are usable by anything that can read a text file, including people.

Encoding complex geometry can be a challenge, however, due to the difficulty of representing multiple vertices concisely. Lack of compression means big datasets have very large file sizes.

Name: GeoJSON
Description:
GeoJSON is a standardized structured text format for describing geometry, attributes, and collections of features.

GeoJSON uses JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) to represent data in a nested structure.

Share.explanation:
GeoJSON is good for sharing data because JSON is native to the browser. GeoJSON is a Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) standard format for geospatial data exchange and many applications are designed to parse it correctly.

Lack of compression means big datasets have very large file sizes.

Name: GPX
Description:
GPS Exchange Format (GPX) is a structured text format for describing waypoints in space-time using Extensible Markup Language (XML). It can also store routes (collections of waypoints) and tracks (collections of routes).

Some platforms extend the format to include attributes beyond a timestamp.

Share.explanation:
A GPX file is good for sharing data between GPS units and GIS platforms.

GIS platforms can typically convert and export GPX files, but generally can't use them directly for visualization, editing, or analysis.

Name: KML / KMZ
Description:
Keyhole Markup Language (KML) is a standardized structured text format for describing feature geometry, attributes, and styling using XML.

KMZ is a zipped collection of KML files for describing complex datasets and styling.

Share.explanation:
A KML/KMZ file is good for for sharing data with Google Earth and some drone platforms that expect it.

Because it has an OGC standard specification, GIS platforms can typically convert, export, and display KML/KMZ files, but generally can't use them directly for editing or analysis.

Display.explanation:
A KML/KMZ file is usable for display because it contain XML tags for styling.

The styling options are limited, however, and can be difficult to use.

Name: DWG / DXF
Description:
DWG (drawing) and DXF (Drawing Exchange Format) are file formats for storing geometry, attributes, and metadata. Both formats are designed for CAD systems.

DWG files are binary, and while DXF files can be ASCII text, they use encoded data that is not human-readable.

Share.explanation:
DWG and DXF files are good for sharing data between CAD and GIS platforms. Because the formats are largely controlled by Autodesk, 100% interoperability has been technically and legally challenging.

GIS platforms can typically convert, export, and view these files, but generally can't use them directly for editing or analysis.

Name: File geodatabase
Description:
A file geodatabase is a directory with many individual files that encode geospatial data.

Esri designed it as a replacement for the personal geodatabases, which was the original replacement for shapefiles.

Esri.explanation:
A file geodatabase is good to use in ArcGIS Pro because it is the default and supports many geodatabase capabilities without the need for a full RDBMS.

Many other tools in the Esri ecosystem will accept a file geodatabase as input or produce one as output.

Analysis.explanation:
A File geodatabase is useable for analysis of small datasets within ArcGIS Pro.

The lack of columnar storage or a sophisticated query optimizer, however, make it less good for large datasets.

Records.explanation:
A file geodatabase is good as a system of record within ArcGIS Pro because it uses indexing for fast individual record reads and has ACID-compliant updates.

Lack of full support outside ArcGIS Pro, however, makes it less useful as a system of record in other contexts.

Share.explanation:
A file geodatabase is good for sharing data across ArcGIS products because it is highly familiar to users. It requires compression to share effectively, which makes them less convenient.

While Esri has published an API for read/write access, file geodatabases are not fully supported outside ArcGIS.

Services.explanation:
A file geodatabase is usable for read-only map services published to ArcGIS Server.

Disk I/O limits its useability for service-based editing workflows.

Name: FlatGeobuf
Description:
FlatGeobuf encodes geospatial data using Flat Buffers and indexed using a Hilbert curve.

This makes FlatGeobuf very fast to query because it can use the index to access just the data for a given location, and use Flat Buffers to read data directly into memory without decompression or deserialization.

Share.explanation:
FlatGeoBuf is usable for sharing read-only data because of its convenient single file format and fast access speed.

Flat Buffers make the file size larger than other binary formats, and it is not universally supported by all GIS platforms out of the box.

Cloud.explanation:
FlatGeobuf is excellent for cloud native GIS because it can be stored cheaply in object storage like S3.

Its Hilbert-curve indexing, use of Flat Buffers, and support for HTTP range requests enable efficient bounding box queries without a server.

Name: GeoParquet
Description:
GeoParquet is an extension of the open standard Parquet binary file format with spatial data types. The format is immutable, which means files cannot be edited in place, only overwritten.

They store data in columns instead of rows, and have extensive metadata on row groups within columns

Analysis.explanation:
GeoParquet files are excellent for analysis because column orientation and row group metadata enable a query to read only the necessary data.

This can dramatically reduce disk I/O and therefore increase analysis speed.

Share.explanation:
GeoParquet is good for sharing read-only data between GIS platforms because it uses sophisticated data compression algorithms to reduce file size.

GIS platforms can usually convert, export, analyze, and display GeoParquet, but the immutable design of GeoParquet makes them unsuitable for editing directly.

Cloud.explanation:
GeoParquet is excellent for cloud native GIS because it can be stored cheaply in object storage like S3.

Its column-oriented storage, row group metadata, and support for HTTP range requests enable efficient queries without a server.

Name: Shapefile
Description:
A shapefile is several files that together represent a spatial dataset. It requires a .shp for the feature geometry, a .shx for the shape index, and a .dbf for the non-spatial attributes.

A shapefile can include optional files, such as .prj for the projection, .cpg for character encoding, .sbn/.sbx for the spatial index, and .xml for metadata.

Share.explanation:
Shapefiles are usable for sharing data with legacy systems that require a shapefile. Useless otherwise.

A format so bad there's an entire webpage dedicated to hating it.

Name: SQLite
Description:
A SQLite file is a storage format readable and writable by applications that implement the SQLite in-process database engine. Spatial SQLite adds geospatial datatypes.

The the most common spatial SQLite implementations are the OGC-standard GeoPackage and Esri's mobile geodatabase.

Esri.explanation: Implemented as a mobile geodatabase, spatial SQLite is good to use for offline data editing with ArcGIS Field Maps and for solo work in ArcGIS Pro.

Analysis.explanation:
Spatial SQLite is good for analysis of small or medium size geospatial datasets.

The lack of columnar storage or a sophisticated query optimizer, however, make it less good for large datasets.

Records.explanation:
SQLite is good as a system of record because it uses indexing for fast individual record reads and has ACID-compliant updates.

It is limited by the inability to support multiple simultaneous editors.

Share.explanation:
Implemented as a GeoPackage, spatial SQLite is excellent for sharing data because it is an OGC-standard format that GIS platforms can use directly for conversion, export, analysis, editing, and display.

A GeoPackage is a single file that holds terabytes of data and doesn't cut off field names. Use it instead of a shapefile.

Name: MVT
Description:
The Mapbox Vector Tiles (MVT) format encodes the geometry, styling, and feature attributes in Protocol Buffer (pbf).

It generally only includes labels and not a full set of feature attributes.

Esri.explanation:
Implemented as vector tiles, MVT is excellent to use in ArcGIS for static visualization layers like basemaps because ArcGIS applications are designed to take advantage of their benefits.

The official Esri basemaps use vector tiles.

Display.explanation:
MVT is excellent to use for display because it uses lossy multi-resolution overviews to render geometry very quickly at different scales.

MVT can have different styling applied to it to create different looking layers from the same underlying tile data.

Services.explanation:
MVT is excellent for tile services because the fast display offsets service latency.

GeoServer and other open-source platforms support MVT for static visualization services. As a vector tile service in ArcGIS Enterprise or ArcGIS Online, MVT is Esri's recommended way to expose static vector data for display.

Name: PMTiles
Description:
The PMTiles format stores tiled data at multiple resolutions and scales in a single archive.

The tile data is indexed with a Hilbert curve, allowing tiles for a given location to be accessed via HTTP range requests.

Display.explanation: As a container for tiled data, PMTiles is excellent for display because it leverages the benefits of the underlying format, such as MVT.

Cloud.explanation:
PMTiles is good for cloud native GIS because it can be stored cheaply in object storage like S3

Support for HTTPS range requests means it can also be streamed to web maps without needing a server.

Name: Cloud data warehouse
Description:
A cloud data warehouse is an elastic query compute engine that accesses data in separate object storage. You pay-as-you-go for analysis instead of keeping a database running.

The most common implementations are Snowflake, Amazon Redshift, and Google BigQuery.

Analysis.explanation:
A cloud data warehouse is good for big data analysis because it stores data in a columnar format that is highly optimized for the service provider's specific query engine.

That benefit comes at the cost of increased complexity.

Cloud.explanation:
A cloud data warehouse is good for cloud native big data workflows because you can scale the warehouse arbitrarily large without any idle resources. You only pay for the storage and compute you actually use.

That benefit comes at the cost of increased complexity.

Name: Document store
Description:
A document store is a distributed NoSQL database for storing and indexing JSON documents. It can use spatiotemporal indexing to make it useful for GIS workflows.

The most common implementations are Elasticsearch and OpenSearch.

Esri.explanation:
Implemented as the spatiotemporal big data store, a document store is used for persisting real-time data in ArcGIS Enterprise.

It is useful when the volume or velocity of data is too high for the relational store to handle effectively.

Analysis.explanation:
A document store with a spatiotemporal index is good for analysis that is based on search or aggregation.

The sophisticated indexing makes it possible to return queries across billions of documents very quickly.

Services.explanation: A document store is good for exposing data as services because querying the store is generally done through REST web APIs by default.

Name: Graph database
Description:
A graph database is a type of NoSQL database that tracks entities and their relationships.

The most common implementations are Neo4j and ArangoDB

Esri.explanation:
A graph database is used to support ArcGIS Knowledge graphs.

While this is a relatively niche use case, it cannot be done without a graph database.

Analysis.explanation:
A graph database is good for analysis that can be modeled as a graph problem.

While not a common GIS workflow, this type of analysis is useful when entities have both a spatial and non-spatial relationship, such as supply chains.

Records.explanation:
A graph database is used for systems of record when data is best modeled as entities and relationships.

Indexing and entity relationships mean a graph database typically has fast record access and typically ACID-compliant updates.

Services.explanation:
A graph database is used to expose entity-relationship data as an ArcGIS Knowledge graph service.

It is not common to see a graph database used for other kinds of geospatial services.

Name: RDBMS
Description:
A relational database managment system (RDBMS) is software for creating a relational database. Spatial relational databases add spatial datatypes

The most common RDBMS implementations are PostgreSQL, Oracle, Microsoft SQL Server. Esri's enterprise geodatabase and relational store are created in an RDBMS

Esri.explanation:
Implemented as an enterprise geodatabase, a spatial relational database is excellent to use with ArcGIS because it adds schemas and stored procedures specific to ArcGIS.

Implemented as a relational store, it holds data for hosted feature layers in ArcGIS Online or ArcGIS Enterprise.

Analysis.explanation:
A spatial relational database is good for analysis because it has a sophisticated engine for optimizing queries with spatial predicates.

The lack of columnar storage, however, can slow down analysis for the very largest datasets.

Records.explanation:
A spatial relational database is excellent for systems of record because it uses robust indexing for fast lookups, ACID-compliant updates for safe updates, and archiving for viewing historic data.

Esri enterprise geodatabases also use versioning for multi-user editing.

Services.explanation:
A relational database is excellent for exposing data as services because it is designed for multiple simultaneous connections.

A spatial relational database supports OGC WMS and WFS formats, and Esri enterprise geodatabases additionally support ArcGIS map and feature services.

Cloud.explanation:
A relational database is good for cloud native GIS when deployed using a Database-as-a-Service (DBaaS) such as Amazon Aurora, Azure SQL Database, or Google Cloud SQL.

DBaaS enables easier scaling and offloads maintenance tasks to the service provider. The trade off for this flexibility is increased operating costs.
